name: L-Tryptophan

lead: Tryptophan is an essential amino acid found in meat, dairy, eggs, nuts and seeds, and the starting material for serotonin, melatonin and niacin. As a supplement it is used for sleep and mood, with looksmaxxing users linking better sleep to clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face.

Most dietary tryptophan goes down the kynurenine pathway, while a smaller share becomes serotonin and melatonin. A 2001 Cochrane review found only two eligible studies with 64 participants and judged the evidence insufficient, and a 2017 American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline advises against its use for insomnia; appearance outcomes have not been studied.

paras: People take it as capsules or powder in the evening, often away from protein-heavy meals and as part of a wind-down routine. Sleep effects are judged over days to weeks.

Side effects include nausea, drowsiness and headache; combining with SSRIs or MAOIs can cause serotonin syndrome. A 1989 outbreak of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome, traced largely to contaminated batches, led to US restrictions that were lifted in 2001.

angle.text: L-tryptophan is taken as a serotonin and melatonin precursor for sleep and mood, on the theory that better sleep shows up as clearer skin, less puffiness and a more rested face. A 2001 Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for sleep, and appearance has not been studied.

lead: Tryptophan is an essential amino acid that humans cannot make and must obtain from protein foods such as meat, dairy, eggs, nuts and seeds. Besides building proteins it is a precursor of serotonin, melatonin and niacin [1]. Frederick Hopkins first isolated it in 1901 from casein [1].

As a supplement it is marketed for sleep, mood and anxiety. Wikipedia reports the supporting evidence as weak: a 2001 Cochrane review found only two eligible studies with 64 participants and judged evidence insufficient, and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's 2017 guideline advises against its use for insomnia [1]. In 1989 supplements were linked to an outbreak of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome (EMS) [1].
infobox: Over-the-counter supplement in US and UK; prescription in some European countries [1]

paras: Over 95% of tryptophan is broken down through the kynurenine pathway; smaller amounts become serotonin and, from it, melatonin [1]. Gut microbes also transform tryptophan into metabolites such as indoles that interact with host immune receptors [2][3].

Reported effects include nausea, diarrhea, drowsiness, lightheadedness, headache, dry mouth and blurred vision, and combination with MAOIs or SSRIs can cause serotonin syndrome [1]. The US drug label for one product lists use for temporary relief of anxiety, mood swings and sleeplessness and advises pregnant or breastfeeding users to consult a professional [4].

More than 1,500 US cases of eosinophilia-myalgia syndrome and at least 37 deaths were reported, linked to tryptophan supplements, which the FDA recalled in 1989 and largely barred from public sale in 1990 [1]. Later studies traced the outbreak to contaminated batches from one Japanese manufacturer, though some researchers suspect tryptophan itself may contribute [1]. The FDA eased restrictions in 2001 and maintained import limits until 2005 [1].

The 2001 Cochrane review of tryptophan for depression found two eligible studies (64 participants) and insufficient evidence [1], and the 2017 AASM guideline advises against it for insomnia [1]. Registered trials found are mostly nutritional: tryptophan requirements in adults and children [5][6], absorption from foods [7], and dietary tryptophan and aryl hydrocarbon receptor activation [8]. No studies found that test it for appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: FDA eases restrictions; imports limited until 2005 [1]
